book.title: Dirty Work: Essential Jobs and the Hidden Toll of Inequality in America

evidence: trade publisher signal: Farrar, Straus and Giroux / Macmillan

argument.statement: Society increasingly distances itself from morally questionable essential work, while the psychological and emotional burdens fall disproportionately on less privileged workers.

book.rationale: The book addresses societal issues surrounding essential yet morally complex occupations, exploring the cultural and political dimensions of labor and inequality in America.
book.summary: A groundbreaking, urgent report from the front lines of "dirty work"—the work that society considers essential but morally compromised Drone pilots who carry out targeted assassinations. Undocumented immigrants who man the “kill floors” of industrial slaughterhouses. Guards who patrol the wards of America’s most violent and abusive prisons. In Dirty Work, Eyal Press offers a paradigm-shifting view of the moral landscape of contemporary America through the stories of people who perform society’s most ethically troubling jobs. As Press shows, we are increasingly shielded and distanced from an array of morally questionable activities that other, less privileged people perform in our name. The COVID-19 pandemic has drawn unprecedented attention to the issue of “essential workers,” and to the health and safety risks to which workers in prisons and slaughterhouses are exposed. But Dirty Work examines another, less familiar set of occupational hazards: psychological and emotional hardships such as stigma, shame, PTSD, and moral injury. These burdens fall disproportionately on low-income workers, undocumented immigrants, women, and people of color.
